Search summary of an info board: measured 2003, largest 44.6 m high, 1.39 m breast-height diameter (about 437 cm girth); figure NOT seen on a fetched page, so unusable. Not a Naturdenkmal (only the Baumgruppe vor Schloss Solitude, ash plus maples, is) so no per-tree official register record; no exact coordinate. Cannot end rich.

Strong tree: 7.55 m girth at breast height, 24 m, about 400 years (Rainer Lippert, monumentale-eichen.de, measured 2022, fetched; monumentaltrees.com 7.65 m cross-check not fetched). Also called Christophseiche; ten oaks over 6 m in the reserve (Alte Eiche 7.10 m, Saufang-Eiche 6.80 m, Bernhards-Eiche 6.65 m, Adlereiche 6.55 m). Fails RICH and honesty: stands in the Naturschutzgebiet Rotwildpark (no per-tree register record), a search summary says no footpath leads to it, and a survey notes rotting sapwood; no open licence photo found; access to the exact tree unsettled. Lead with coordinate for a session that can settle paths from OSM.

Stuttgarter Zeitung 2016: almost sixty sequoias behind the Wilhelma main entrance, tallest 37 m, girth 4.20 m (Stuttgarter Nachrichten gives 4.7 m circumference for the thickest: conflict, both seen only as article/search text, the NN page 404s now). Paid entry zoo and botanic garden, owner of the ground is the source for access, but no per-tree register record and no coordinate. Cannot end rich.

Dronfieldpark is in Sindelfingen (Böblingen district), a separate town roughly 15 km from Stuttgart's centre, picked up by the brief's 15 km Wikidata radius sweep rather than being inside city limits. Publishing it under Stuttgart would misstate its location; it is a candidate for a future Sindelfingen page instead, not this one.

Location uncertain: the Mietholz is a strictly protected Bannwald forest reserve described as separated from the Sindelfingen forest by the A8/A81 motorway and as the forest reserve closest to Stuttgart, which suggests it may sit outside Stuttgart's own municipal boundary (unconfirmed either way this pass). Access is also a concern independent of the boundary question: sources describe the oak as 'deep within the forest, hidden off marked trails', and a Bannwald (strict forest nature reserve) commonly restricts visitors to marked paths, which would put the tree itself off-limits even if the general area is open. Needs a boundary check and an access answer (does a permissive path reach it, per the OSM-access technique in BRIEF_RESEARCH.md) before it can be verified either way.

blocked.name: The Max-Eyth-See Oak
blocked.story:
Stuttgart's protection ordinance obliges the city to have this oak examined once a year for its health and safety. That is a level of attention most trees never get, and it comes with the natural monument status the pedunculate oak was given in June 2003, for its character and for its value as habitat.

It stands on the shore of the Max-Eyth-See, which is not a natural lake at all. The water sits in a gravel quarry that was worked out and then flooded in 1935, put under landscape protection in 1961, and has been Stuttgart's biggest outdoor escape ever since. On a warm weekend up to 15,000 people come out here, and the paths run the whole way round the water.

So this oak has spent its recent decades as a piece of public furniture, which is a harder life than a forest. It has watched a working pit turn into a lake, then into a protected landscape, then into a place where a good part of the city spends its Sundays.

What no source will tell us is how old it is. Nobody has recorded an age or a girth, so we do not know whether it stood here before the quarry filled with water or arrived with the park. A photograph taken in May 2022 puts it firmly alive and standing. If you know its age, tell us.
blocked.access: In the public lakeside park around the Max-Eyth-See, a free and heavily used recreation area with paths all around the lake; open at all times, no ticket.
blocked.transport: Stadtbahn U14 to the Max-Eyth-See stop, a few minutes' walk

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

blocked.removed_reason: Dead. Its own Commons photograph, dated 21 May 2022 and taken 27 m from our pin, shows every limb sawn off with fresh cut faces and not one leaf on the trunk while everything around it stands in full spring green. Stuttgart's ordinance protected it partly 'for its value as habitat', which is why a dead oak is left standing there. Removed under the rule that a dead tree is never a collectible entry. If the city ever plants a successor at the Max-Eyth-See, this is where the research is.
